title: 基于自适应的遗传算法的参数优化
abstract: This paper introduces a novel genetic algorithm (GA) based on an adaptive adjustment mechanism to enhance search efficiency and result quality. Traditional genetic algorithms often rely on fixed parameters, limiting their ability to adapt to complex, noisy environments. This work proposes a dynamic adjustment strategy that continuously refines the GA's parameters based on the optimization objective and environmental noise. The proposed algorithm demonstrates improved performance in a variety of optimization tasks, particularly when dealing with non-stationary problems. This advancement addresses a crucial limitation in genetic algorithm design and offers a more robust and adaptable approach to parameter optimization.

title: Multi-Dimensional Geometric Data Analysis Adaptive Clustering Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel adaptive clustering algorithm designed for handling multi-dimensional geometric data. Traditional clustering methods often employ fixed cluster coefficients, failing to effectively leverage data distributions and feature relationships. Our algorithm dynamically adjusts cluster coefficients based on these relationships, resulting in significantly improved clustering quality. The core mechanism revolves around a feedback loop that iteratively refines the cluster boundaries, ensuring a more accurate representation of the data's underlying structure. The paper details the algorithm's design, its performance evaluation, and a discussion of its potential applications in diverse geometric data analysis scenarios. The primary focus is on enhancing the robustness and accuracy of clustering results, particularly when dealing with complex geometric datasets.

The proposed protocol offers a significant advancement over existing methods, particularly in terms of security and error correction capabilities.

title: Time-Encoded Multi-Particle Dynamics
abstract: Time-Encoded Multi-Particle Dynamics (TEMPD) represents a novel approach to modeling dynamic biological systems by encoding time-dependent quantum states within particle interactions. This research introduces a framework that leverages quantum entanglement and error correction to simulate complex biological behavior, offering a pathway toward improved prediction of evolutionary processes. The core mechanism involves constructing a multi-particle system, where each particle embodies a biological entity, and applying quantum information encoding to dynamically alter their states based on time. This leads to a more accurate representation of biological processes compared to traditional static models. TEMPD's potential lies in its ability to capture subtle temporal dynamics often overlooked in conventional simulations, providing a robust foundation for understanding and potentially guiding biological evolution.

title: Deploying an AI-Powered Operational Intelligence Platform in Independent Field Service Operations: A Pilot Case Study of FieldMind AI (GFM) with 9Pool Service LLC
abstract: This case study documents the early beta deployment of FieldMind AI (GFM), an AI-powered operational intelligence platform, with 9Pool Service LLC, an independent pool service operator engaged under a complimentary pilot arrangement. We describe the pilot's scope, the functional modules deployed, the operational volume observed, and an illustrative estimate of the administrative time such volume represents under manual workflows. The purpose of this case study is to document real-world deployment conditions and provide a transparent basis for future, more rigorous empirical evaluation of the platform's operational impact.

title: Interpretable machine learning model for predicting the ICU readmission of patients after coronary intervention
abstract: To develop and validate an interpretable machine learning (ML) model integrated with inflammatory indicators for predicting ICU readmission in patients after coronary intervention (PCI/CABG). We used retrospective data from MIMIC-IV (training, 2196 patients) and MIMIC-III (external validation, 1717 patients). Patients aged > 18 years with complete hematological data and < 40% missing data were included in the study. LASSO regression selected 20 clinical variables; nine ML algorithms (e.g., RF, XGBoost) were compared. The optimal model was evaluated using AUC, calibration curves, DCA, and CIC, with SHAP for interpretability. In MIMIC-IV, 674 (30.7%) patients had multiple ICU admissions, and 440 (25.6%) in MIMIC-III. RF outperformed the other models (internal AUC = 0.85, external AUC = 0.706), with balanced accuracy (0.772), sensitivity (0.748), and specificity (0.795). The key predictors included MLR, maximum creatinine levels, invasive procedures, and so on. The model was optimized for 12 variables and deployed online. The RF model achieves moderate predictive performance for ICU readmission risk of post-coronary intervention patients within the same single tertiary hospital across different periods, and SHAP improves model interpretability to facilitate screening high-risk patients. SHAP enhances interpretability, aiding in the early identification of high-risk patients and improving outcomes.

title: Lattice: Enabling Scalable Enclaves for Commercial RISC-V Platforms
abstract: Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) have been extensively adopted to facilitate various security-critical applications. However, in stark contrast to well-established TEE technologies such as Intel SGX, AMD SEV, and ARM TrustZone, the adoption within the emerging RISC-V architecture has seen limited traction. Specifically, existing TEE implementations on current commercial RISC-V hardware face two primary constraints. On one hand, most approaches rely on specific hardware extensions or software firmware, hindering their practicality on real platforms. On the other hand, the intrinsic limits of RISC-V’s Physical Memory Protection (PMP) registers, a key hardware mechanism to achieve memory isolation, have significantly restricted the scalability of these designs. To address the above limitations, in this article, we introduce Lattice , a novel RISC-V TEE framework that enables scalable enclaves on commercial RISC-V platforms with a minimal Trusted Computing Base (TCB). Firstly, for enhanced compatibility and portability, Lattice does not rely on any additional hardware extensions and proposes a non-intrusive Secure Monitor (SM) design for the underlying firmware. Secondly, to fully utilize the system’s available memory, Lattice leverages the Dynamic Physical Memory Permission (DPMP) design to enable the execution of enclaves with non-contiguous physical memory, and decouples the management of enclaves to minimize the size of the TCB. Finally, we evaluate the performance of Lattice under various workloads, including file system I/O, databases, web servers, large language models (LLMs), and different system loads. The experimental results indicate that Lattice achieves performance comparable to other TEE systems.

title: A Reverse Sign Language Dictionary: Open-Vocabulary Sign Recognition from Continuous Signing via Video Captioning and Description Retrieval
abstract: Isolated Sign Language Recognition (ISLR) is conventionally cast as closed-set classification over gloss labels, which cannot generalize to signs unseen in training and ties every deployment to a gloss-annotated lexicon. We instead recognize signs extracted from continuous signing by (1) captioning a sign-level clip into a free-form procedural description of the articulation with an open-weight vision-language model, and (2) retrieving the closest entry from a vocabulary of target descriptions with a multilingual sentence encoder: a reverse sign language dictionary that needs no gloss supervision and admits an open vocabulary. On 1,300 sign-level segments from a Japanese Sign Language (JSL) dialogue corpus annotated with procedural descriptions (against a 2% top-10 chance floor over the 503-entry target vocabulary), fine-tuning the captioner substantially improves seen-class retrieval: language and vision tower fine-tuning raises top-10 retrieval on seen classes from 4.5% (untrained) to 49%, becoming statistically indistinguishable from a standard supervised closed-set classifier (I3D) on two of the three test sets where a closed-set classifier can be evaluated at all. More importantly, unseen-class retrieval also improves significantly over the untrained pipeline (11.5% -> 21.0% top-10, p=0.0094), a regime in which the closed-set classifier cannot participate. A matcher-side empirical upper-bound analysis shows the sentence encoder already recovers close to 100% of paraphrased gold descriptions, locating a gap in captioning quality that we aim to address in future work. To our knowledge this is the first description-based, open-vocabulary sign lookup from continuous signing without gloss supervision, and the first for JSL.

title: Neural Video Compression Based on Deformable Temporal Alignment and Difference-aware Fusion
abstract: In conditional coding-based neural video compression, the quality of temporal context directly affects compression per- formance. Existing methods mostly construct context from prop- agated reference features, but they are vulnerable to motion esti- mation and local alignment errors in regions with complex mo- tion, occlusion, and high-frequency textures, resulting in inaccu- rate temporal information. To address this issue, this paper pro- poses a method combining deformable temporal alignment and difference-aware spatial selective fusion. A Context-aware Tem- poral Alignment Module is used to generate complementary tem- poral context, while a Difference-aware Spatial Selective Fusion module adaptively selects reliable temporal information and sup- presses misalignment. Experiments show that the proposed method achieves certain rate-distortion performance improve- ment over DCVC-DC.

Experiments show that the proposed method achieves certain rate-distortion performance improve- ment over DCVC-DC.

title: Risk and Anomaly Identification for Distribution Network Optimal Operation Based on Reinforcement Learning and Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: Reliable operation of modern distribution networks requires timely identification of operational risks and anomalous events under pervasive uncertainty. In practice, operators must identify risks that are inherent in stochastic yet in-distribution conditions, and anomalies that correspond to out-of-distribution behaviors such as unusual load patterns, extreme weather or cyber-physical attacks. This paper addresses this joint risk and anomaly identification problem for optimal distribution network operation and proposes a deep reinforcement learning framework that is explicitly uncertainty aware. We integrate distributional and Bayesian deep reinforcement learning to realize a second- order uncertainty quantification scheme that decomposes total uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components, which are respectively used to characterize inherent risk and out-of- distribution anomalies. The resulting epistemic estimates drive both exploration during training and out-of-distribution detec- tion with fallback control during deployment, whereas aleatoric estimates are used to characterize intrinsic operational risk. Simulation results demonstrate the performance of our DRL agent and the effectiveness of the uncertainty quantification.

title: Algorithmic Fractal Resonance (AFR)
abstract: This paper presents Algorithmic Fractal Resonance (AFR), a novel algorithm designed to optimize the performance of neural networks through the integration of fractal geometry and complex resonance. We explore a self-organizing process where the network's weights are iteratively refined to induce resonant patterns, ultimately enhancing learning accuracy and reducing overfitting. The core mechanism centers around the creation of a fractal structure that dynamically adjusts to the network's internal state, amplifying key learning signals. This approach offers a departure from traditional gradient descent optimization, promising improved efficiency and accuracy.

title: Adaptive Machine Learning Gradient Descent Strategy
abstract: This paper presents a novel adaptive machine learning gradient descent strategy designed to enhance model precision and efficiency. Traditional gradient descent methods often rely on fixed learning rates and step sizes, failing to effectively adapt to the inherent variability of the data. We propose a framework that dynamically adjusts these parameters based on observed data characteristics, leveraging a dynamic learning rate and optimization step size. This approach significantly improves model performance and streamlines the training process. The core mechanism involves integrating a dynamically adjusted learning rate and optimization step size based on feature similarity and gradients, achieving superior results compared to static gradient descent methods. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the proposed strategy, demonstrating its effectiveness through experimental results.

title: Adaptive Distributed Learning with Epistemic Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: Distributed learning (DL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for training machine learning models across multiple devices, offering advantages in terms of scalability and reduced communication costs. However, many existing DL approaches operate under the simplifying assumption of identical model parameters and gradients, neglecting the inherent heterogeneity in learner performance and knowledge. This paper introduces a novel adaptive distributed learning framework that explicitly addresses this limitation by incorporating epistemic uncertainty quantification. Each learner estimates its own uncertainty—its lack of knowledge—regarding the global model. This uncertainty is then leveraged to dynamically adjust learning rates and aggregation strategies, prioritizing learners with lower uncertainty. The proposed mechanism promotes more robust and efficient convergence by accounting for learner heterogeneity, leading to a more adaptive and effective distributed learning process. The core claim of this work is that current DL approaches often assume identical model parameters and gradients, ignoring inherent differences in learner performance and knowledge. The core mechanism integrates a mechanism for each learner to estimate *epistemic uncertainty* – its own lack of knowledge – regarding the global model. This uncertainty is then used to dynamically adjust learning rates and aggregation strategies, favouring learners with lower uncertainty. Why it is new is explicitly accounts for learner heterogeneity through uncertainty quantification, leading to more robust and efficient convergence.

title: Dynamic Quantum State Cryptography Algorithm Design
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum information cryptography algorithm based on the dynamic evolution of quantum states. Traditional cryptographic methods rely on static keys, while this approach leverages the inherent instability of quantum states to generate keys, enhancing security. The algorithm employs a continuous state transformation process to produce a unique key for each input data. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through a series of simulations and analysis, highlighting its potential for robust encryption. The core mechanism centers around the manipulation of quantum states to achieve key generation and decryption.

title: Decentralized Differential Privacy via Byzantine Fault Tolerance Consensus
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to achieving differential privacy in decentralized networks by integrating Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT) consensus mechanisms. The core idea revolves around a consensus algorithm where each participating node introduces noise to its data before dissemination, with the noise level dynamically calibrated based on the detected Byzantine behavior of other nodes. This method addresses the challenges of maintaining privacy while operating in environments susceptible to malicious or faulty actors. We demonstrate that by leveraging the robustness of BFT, we can guarantee differential privacy without relying on centralized authorities or requiring strict trust assumptions among network participants. The proposed system provides a practical solution for privacy-preserving data sharing in decentralized settings.

title: Automated Theorem Proving with Deep Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Automated theorem proving (ATP) has achieved significant progress over the years, yet it frequently struggles with complex mathematical reasoning and strategic planning. This work introduces a novel approach to ATP leveraging deep reinforcement learning (DRL). The core idea is to train an intelligent agent capable of interacting with a theorem prover, learning optimal strategies for selecting theorems, axioms, and proof tactics. We hypothesize that a DRL agent can surpass human capabilities by learning a more efficient and robust reasoning process. This paper details the architecture of the agent, the reward function design, and the training methodology. Preliminary results demonstrate the potential of this approach to automate theorem proving effectively, suggesting a new paradigm for tackling challenging mathematical problems. The primary goal is to create an agent that can dynamically adapt to the proof process, improving upon the limitations of traditional, rule-based ATP systems.

title: Decentralized Federated Learning with Secure Multi-Party Computation
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to decentralized federated learning (DFL) that leverages secure multi-party computation (SMPC) to guarantee data privacy during collaborative model training. Traditional federated learning methods, while promoting data sharing for model improvement, inherently expose individual datasets to the central server, raising significant privacy concerns. Our framework addresses this limitation by employing SMPC protocols, enabling model updates to be aggregated securely without revealing the underlying data. This approach provides a strong privacy guarantee, combining the benefits of federated learning with robust privacy protection. We present a detailed description of the system architecture, the SMPC protocols utilized, and the mathematical formulation underpinning the aggregation process. The core claim of this work is the ability to enable collaborative model training across multiple parties without revealing individual data. The core mechanism relies on implementing a federated learning framework based on secure multi-party computation protocols, where model updates are aggregated securely without exposing the underlying data. This research represents a significant advancement in the field of privacy-preserving machine learning.

title: Quantum-Inspired Secure Multi-Party Computation via Tensor Networks
abstract: Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) aims to enable computation on sensitive data without revealing the individual inputs of the participants. Traditional SMPC protocols often suffer from significant computational overhead, particularly in terms of communication complexity. This paper proposes a novel approach to SMPC leveraging tensor network techniques inspired by quantum computation. We demonstrate that tensor networks can efficiently represent and manipulate the necessary data structures for SMPC protocols, leading to a substantial reduction in communication overhead and improved scalability. Our method utilizes the inherent structure of tensor networks to minimize the number of exchanges required during computation, effectively addressing a key bottleneck in existing SMPC implementations. We outline the theoretical foundations and present a framework for designing SMPC protocols using tensor networks. This work represents a significant step towards practical and efficient SMPC solutions, particularly for large-scale datasets and complex computations. The key contribution lies in the application of quantum-inspired techniques to solve classical computational problems, specifically within the context of secure computation.

title: Qubits of a Feather, Flawed Together: A Interdisciplinary Mapping Review of Quantum Computing Architectures Compared
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Quantum Computing Architectures Compared in the context of Physics. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of quantum computing and qubits as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Physics.

An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Physics.

title: Colorectal Lesion diagnosis using transformer and deep learning with multiscale feature interface
abstract: Colorectal cancer is the third most common malignancy worldwide. Manual screening requires expertise and resources. However, advancements in AI (artificial intelligence) have reduced the computation burden and time. Machine and deep learning have recently been used to diagnose colorectal lesions. The requirement of handcrafted features makes machine learning models expertise-dependent. At the same time, classical CNN (convolutional neural network) miss the global attention of the features. This work presents CDCTNet (colorectal diagnosis convolution transformer network), a hierarchical model for colorectal disease detection. Our model utilized two convolution blocks for the local high-dimensional spatial features from the lesion. In addition, the ViT encoder is used in parallel with the CNN block to provide a global correlation of the feature map. Furthermore, we designed an IEM block for the interaction of the features between the convolution block and ViT encoder to improve the attention on the features. The CDCTNet is evaluated on Kather and Kvasir datasets and obtained a precision and Kappa score of 96.60% and 95.02%, respectively. At the same time, CDCTNet has recall and F1 scores of 98.08% and 97.94%.

title: Foundations
abstract: This chapter introduces the conceptual and mathematical underpinnings of quantum computing (QC), explains how qubits differ from classical bits, and highlights the central challenges of coherence and error correction. It also situates QC within its historical trajectory—from Feynman's early vision in the 1980s to breakthroughs such as Shor's algorithm, Grover's search, and the emergence of various QC platforms such as superconducting and ion-trap systems. The chapter shows how to compare computing performance (complexity theory). Complexity theory is used to evaluate how the performance changes when different algorithms solve problems as they scale in size. By contrasting classical and quantum logic, it emphasizes why certain problems remain intractable for classical machines but could become solvable within the quantum paradigm. Measurement-based quantum computing operates by preparing an entangled resource state and then performing a sequence of measurements on individual qubits.

title: Nested Inductive Bias Framework for SPD Manifold Learning
abstract: In Geometric Deep Learning, inductive biases serve two primary functions: enforcing manifold constraints and embedding relational priors. Currently, representation learning on SPD manifolds frequently relies on pullback Euclidean metrics, such as the Log-Euclidean Metric, to satisfy the former. While computationally efficient in avoiding domain boundary violations, these metrics induce a flat geometry that may fail to capture the intrinsic relational priors of datasets. While metrics such as the Poincaré metric are widely utilized to induce domain-aligned relational priors, generalizing them from standard vector representations to the SPD manifold has remained a challenge. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Nested Inductive Bias framework that utilizes a two-stage diffeomorphic composition to formally pull back non-Euclidean target geometries onto the SPD manifold. This framework enables the construction of curvature-aligned Riemannian classifiers that simultaneously respect matrix constraints and the latent relational geometry of the data. Empirical evaluations on kinematic and signal processing benchmarks, together with synthetic experiments, demonstrate that deep manifold networks experience degradation in class separability unless the metric curvature aligns with the intrinsic data distribution. Furthermore, for standard vectorized architectures, we propose the Rational Conformal Metric (RCM), designed to establish state-of-the-art geometric robustness against outliers by bounding the representation space.

title: Adaptive Vision-Language Grasping via Composable Foundation Priors and Generalizable Grasp Synthesis
abstract: This paper proposes AdaRoboVLG, a task-adaptive Vision-Language-Grasp (VLG) framework that supports generalizable grasp synthesis across different robotic hands. Unlike existing VLG methods that tightly couple foundation models with end-to-end grasp policies, AdaRoboVLG learns an efficient generalizable base policy that generates and evaluates physically feasible grasp candidates through explicit kinematic mapping and force-closure-based stability estimation, while offloading task-dependent understanding to specialized foundation-model modules. These modules provide composable priors that are integrated into the grasp synthesis process, enabling contextually adaptive grasp synthesis without retraining the underlying grasp policy. Through extensive simulation and real-world experiments, we demonstrate that (i) the base policy exhibits efficient learning and strong cross-hand generalization, (ii) the framework effectively incorporates spatial, cognitive, and temporal priors to address three representative grasping challenges without compromising grasp synthesis performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, and (iii) these priors can operate jointly to enable functional grasping in cluttered and dynamic environments. These results indicate that decoupling physical grasp synthesis from task-dependent understanding provides a scalable paradigm for robotic grasping, allowing future advances in foundation models to be directly translated into improved grasp capabilities without redesigning or retraining the underlying grasp policy. Supplementary videos are available at https://adarobovlg.github.io/

title: Tight Heavy-Tailed Complexity Bounds for Optimizing Polyak--Łojasiewicz Objectives
abstract: We study optimizing $L$-smooth and $μ$-Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) objectives with unbiased stochastic gradients under $α$-heavy-tailed noise ($1<α\le 2$). In the unrestricted high-dimensional setting, we establish the noise-adaptive lower bound for attaining $ε$-suboptimal function value. Under the generalized mirror-PL condition, we propose a centered-clipped mirror-descent method that achieves a high-probability upper bound matching the lower bound up to logarithmic factors. We further provide the improved tight stochastic complexity in fixed dimensions.

title: DNative-Twin: Decision Graphs and Digital Twins for Reconstructable Agentic Decisions
abstract: AI agents increasingly gather evidence, invoke tools, apply constraints, and produce decisions that people or software may commit to action. A final output alone cannot show which evidence, tool state, rule, authorization, or action path produced it. We present DNative-Twin, a graph-native digital twin that records a committed agentic decision as a typed trajectory and re-executes its decision mechanism under declared conditions. The graph links the state observed by the agent, the path it followed, and the authority behind the resulting action. The twin synchronizes this information, replays the mechanism in isolation, and compares it under controlled changes. We instantiate the framework in enterprise decision processes using three public process logs and controlled replay suites. The experiments identify a specific failure: graph structure localizes represented changes but cannot determine the consequence of an unobserved tool state. In a three-condition controlled experiment with 300 injected instances, unresolved-divergence recall increased from 0 to 0.667 when replay-contract state was added and to 1.0 when verification results were also available; the held-out set contained no critical-class instance. Across 500--5,000 BPI 2020 cases, median end-to-end time increased from 0.794 to 8.889 seconds on the reported platform. These results separate the roles of graph structure, replay context, and verification evidence in reviewing a decision mechanism.

title: Residual Optimal Transport-Based Experts Collaboration Towards Modality-Aware Infrared-Visible Object Detection
abstract: Infrared-visible object detection (IVOD) integrates complementary evidence from visible and infrared sensors for reliable perception in challenging scenes. In practice, sensors may fail or drop frames, leaving one modality unavailable or intermittent. Existing methods for IVOD assume both modalities are always present, and fixed fusion collapses when one stream is missing. Furthermore, it remains a critical challenge to reliably estimate semantic correlation across heterogeneous modalities, especially under spectral distribution discrepancy. We present FlexibleFusion, a unified and adaptive method that flexibly allocates integration pathways and fusion strength, operating seamlessly across complete and missing-modality regimes. At its core, the Modality-Aware Experts Collaboration (MAEC) mechanism selectively activates and aggregates cross-modal or intra-modal expert pathways. It allows cross-modal fusion when full modalities are available and falls back to self-fusion under missing conditions. Additionally, we design Residual Self-Paced Entropic Optimal Transport (RSPEOT) to align heterogeneous feature distributions from a transport perspective. Instead of relying on the fixed sparsity coefficient in standard entropic optimal transport (EOT), RSPEOT introduces a residual-driven self-paced update that prioritizes reliable matches and progressively refines harder ones. This design alleviates the additional optimization burden of standard EOT while preserving reliable semantic alignment. Comprehensive experiments under complete and missing-modality protocols show consistent performance across arbitrary modality configurations. Code will be released upon publication.

title: Geometry-Aware Graph Construction via Adaptive Spectral Bandwidth Control
abstract: Kernelized graph methods - spectral clustering, diffusion maps, and sparse kernel -regression graphs - that use Gaussian kernels depend on the choice of Gaussian bandwidth sigma, which governs the spectral character of the local kernel operator. When sigma is too small, the kernel overestimates local complexity and treats each sample as an independent direction; when sigma is too large, the kernel collapses multiple directions together, the condition number diverges, and all geometric discrimination is lost. We propose a choice of scale to make the spectral complexity of the kernel consistent with the intrinsic complexity of the underlying manifold. We propose a per-node bandwidth criterion that operationalizes this principle by jointly matching the kernel's effective rank to the local intrinsic dimension estimated via minimum spanning tree, anchoring the search in the manifold-consistent log-log scaling regime. We evaluate SSL embeddings from six encoders on CIFAR-100, showing that adaptive bandwidth consistently improves leave-one-out (LOO) classification and label propagation (LP) accuracy over fixed-bandwidth methods and competing adaptive methods.

title: Selective Forgetting in LLMs
abstract: Executive Summary This work approaches the problem of selectively forgetting knowledge from a large language model (LLM) for the purposes of safety, copyright, security, or otherwise. Also known as machine unlearning, this entails training a model to forget certain elements of the dataset on which it was trained. Unlearning methods must be evaluated both in terms of the extent to which the information has successfully been forgotten, and the performance of the unlearned model on the remaining (retained) data. We build on the work of TOFU (Task of Fictitious Unlearning) [21], which provides a dataset and benchmark for evaluating unlearning techniques. We create a new, TOFU-inspired question–answer dataset for the task of machine unlearning. The new dataset includes 10,500 question–answer pairs relating to over 1,000 distinct, synthetic entities of several types. Each question–answer pair is tagged with the entities it refers to, with the graph representation of our dataset containing over 2,600 edges between different entities. We perform two experiments with our dataset. The first experiment aims to capture whether the difficulty of forgetting a concept from a LLM depends on its granularity. For example, is unlearning more likely to be successful if forgetting a single book, rather than the book's author (as an author is connected to multiple books)? We find that granularity does not have a tangible effect on model performance in our dataset. There may be a small effect from granularity on the difficulty of forgetting, but this is not statistically significant across our results. Our second experiment explores the knock-on effect of forgetting a relationship between two entities. For example, if unlearning has been run on a model to forget only who wrote a book, but not the book or author themselves, is the model worse at responding to other questions about that book or author? We find that the model performance is lower on questions that contain the entities pertained in the relationship, than on those that do not. 1

title: Quantum-Accelerated Differential Equation Solver
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum algorithm designed to accelerate the solution of differential equations. Traditional numerical methods often struggle with the computational complexity of differential equations, particularly for high-dimensional problems. We propose a quantum algorithm that leverages quantum superposition and entanglement to achieve exponential speedups in solution finding, offering a potential paradigm shift in computational capabilities. The core mechanism centers around exploiting quantum superposition to represent multiple solution paths concurrently, dramatically reducing the computational resources required for each solution. We detail the algorithm's design, the theoretical analysis underpinning its performance, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating its efficacy. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and potential applications of this technology.

title: Self-Adaptive Dynamic Information Entropy Adjustment Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive dynamic information entropy adjustment algorithm designed to enhance model information transmission and expression. Traditional methods often rely on manual parameter tuning, which can be time-consuming and suboptimal. This algorithm dynamically adjusts the information entropy adjustment parameters to optimize model performance. The core mechanism involves a sophisticated iterative process that analyzes and adjusts the entropy level based on the model's learned representation and its ability to generalize. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through a series of experiments on various machine learning tasks, showcasing improved accuracy and generalization capabilities compared to existing approaches. The paper explores the theoretical underpinnings of the algorithm and provides a detailed implementation of the core components.

title: Quantum Topology Network Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum topology network optimization algorithm, leveraging quantum entanglement and quantum simulation to enable complex system adaptation and self-healing capabilities. Traditional quantum network optimization methods are often static, necessitating adjustments that may not consistently yield optimal results. Our proposed algorithm utilizes quantum entanglement to dynamically adjust network parameters, fostering resilience and adaptability within the system. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through a series of simulations, showcasing improved performance in complex, dynamic scenarios. The core mechanism involves a quantum-enhanced feedback loop that continuously monitors and adjusts network topology, maximizing system stability and responsiveness. Keywords: Quantum Topology, Network Optimization, Quantum Entanglement, Quantum Simulation, Self-Healing Systems, Adaptive Networks.

title: Adaptive Topological Structure Evolution
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive topology evolution system based on evolutionary algorithms and self-adaptive topology. The core principle is to iteratively optimize the topology of a system, driven by evolutionary algorithms, to enable complex system adaptation and self-repair capabilities. We present a novel framework that leverages genetic algorithms to dynamically adjust the topology, responding to environmental changes. The paper details the system's architecture, the evolutionary process, and its potential applications in various domains, including robotics, materials science, and biological systems. This approach offers a significant advancement over static topology approaches by introducing a dynamic and adaptive mechanism.

title: AutoPersona: Proactively Resolving Implicit Requirements in Tasks through Structured Personalized Memory
abstract: As agents increasingly undertake long-horizon personal assistant tasks in concrete application scenarios, personalized memory should support more than passive storage and retrieval. It should also proactively recover implicit requirements in tasks, determine whether prior experience is applicable to the current task, and identify information gaps before they affect task execution. Existing memory systems typically preserve user-agent interaction trajectories, but they lack joint modeling of environment-user-agent interactions and do not learn how memory should influence future actions. We present AutoPersona, a proactive personalized memory framework for resolving implicit requirements during task execution. AutoPersona organizes continual interactions into three complementary memory layers: Trajectory Memory preserves traceable interaction records and task execution histories; Workspace Memory captures user-environment interactions, application states, and task-specific information; and Persona Memory stores user information, preferences, and personalized assistance strategies. A dedicated PersonaAgent proactively utilizes these memories by completing evidence-supported implicit constraints, asking targeted clarification questions when existing memory is insufficient for reliable inference, and injecting personalized guidance into relevant task nodes. Building upon supervised fine-tuning, we use reinforcement learning to jointly optimize personalized memory summarization and clarification of implicit requirements. Experiments on Persona2Web, PersonaMem-v2, and Pi-Bench demonstrate that AutoPersona's structured personalized memory and proactive memory utilization effectively improve task execution performance, personalization consistency, and execution efficiency.

title: Formal Model of Collective Intelligence in Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: This paper presents a formal model for collective intelligence within multi-agent systems (MAS). The core claim is that a rigorous mathematical representation, employing agent-based modeling and information theory, can effectively capture the emergent properties characteristic of collective intelligence. The model centers on agents engaging in communication and learning processes, driven by information gathered through interactions and observations. Emphasis is placed on the propagation of knowledge and the subsequent formation of consensus. Unlike existing descriptive models, this work offers a mathematically precise account of collective intelligence, providing a foundation for analysis and design of intelligent systems. The model is defined using agent states, communication probabilities, learning rules, and consensus mechanisms. Key equations and notations are presented to illustrate the model's structure and operational dynamics. The model's utility is discussed in terms of understanding and potentially influencing collective decision-making processes in complex systems.

title: 基于自适应混沌的几何拓扑的量子计算模型
abstract: Quantum computing is a rapidly advancing field with the potential to revolutionize various industries, including medicine, materials science, and cryptography. However, current quantum computing architectures face significant challenges, primarily related to qubit stability, error correction, and scalability. This research explores a novel approach to quantum computation utilizing a dynamically evolving geometric topology, specifically based on self-adaptive chaos. We propose a model that leverages the inherent unpredictability of chaotic systems to enhance quantum computation's efficiency, robustness, and overall utilization. This method aims to overcome limitations inherent in traditional static quantum algorithms. The core mechanism focuses on dynamically adjusting parameters within a chaotic environment, enabling a more adaptive and resilient quantum circuit. This represents a significant departure from conventional approaches, offering a potential pathway to more effective and scalable quantum technologies.

title: Differential Privacy via Randomized Graph Embedding
abstract: This paper introduces a novel method for achieving differential privacy during graph embedding, termed Randomized Graph Embedding. The core idea revolves around directly injecting noise into the graph structure itself, rather than relying on traditional embedding techniques that often expose sensitive node attributes. Our approach utilizes a randomized edge perturbation strategy, where edges are modified based on a carefully managed privacy budget. This allows us to guarantee differential privacy while maintaining the overall structural properties of the graph. The key contribution lies in providing a practical and effective framework for protecting individual node information within graph datasets, addressing a critical challenge in leveraging graph data for analysis and machine learning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a theoretical analysis and outline its potential applications in various domains where privacy preservation is paramount. The method is formally defined, and its privacy guarantees are quantified using differential privacy metrics.

title: Based on Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) Distributed Denial of Service Attack Defense
abstract: This paper presents a novel defense mechanism against Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks specifically tailored for Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) systems. The core claim is the design of a new distributed DDoS attack defense mechanism leveraging the inherent properties of QKD. The proposed mechanism constructs a distributed secure network based on the secure key transmission of QKD, effectively mitigating the impact of DDoS attacks. This approach enhances network security and reliability by exploiting the quantum nature of the key exchange process. The detailed formulation of the defense strategy, including key rate monitoring, redundancy management, and adaptive protocol switching, are presented. The proposed system aims to provide a robust defense against sophisticated DDoS attacks that target QKD systems, ensuring the continued confidentiality and integrity of key exchange. The system's architecture is outlined, and the mathematical models used for key rate analysis and attack mitigation are described. Finally, future research directions focusing on the integration of machine learning for dynamic threat detection are discussed.

We introduce a self-adaptive graph neural network architecture that learns node relationships to dynamically adjust connection weights, resulting in more efficient model training and prediction. The core mechanism leverages a continuous, learning-based approach to optimize node connections, addressing the limitations of fixed parameter approaches. This work demonstrates the superior performance of our method through comprehensive experimental evaluations on benchmark datasets, showcasing significant improvements in model accuracy and training time.

title: Quantum Entanglement Entropy Measurement in Quantum Computing
abstract: This paper investigates the critical role of entanglement entropy measurement in advancing quantum computing. We propose a novel methodology for precisely quantifying entanglement entropy within quantum systems, recognizing its significance as a key performance indicator for assessing both the quality and scalability of quantum algorithms and hardware. The core of the work focuses on developing a high-precision and efficient measurement technique, addressing the current limitations in entanglement entropy characterization. Specifically, we explore methods for minimizing measurement errors and maximizing the information obtained from entanglement entropy measurements. The theoretical framework presented allows for a deeper understanding of how entanglement entropy relates to computational complexity and provides a basis for optimizing quantum algorithms and designing more robust quantum computing architectures. Ultimately, this research contributes to overcoming a significant bottleneck in the field and paves the way for practical, fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Dynamic Symbolic Regression with Evolutionary Proof-of-Concept
abstract: Symbolic regression is a powerful technique for discovering mathematical relationships from data. However, its reliance on exhaustive search and the potential for overfitting often lead to unstable and unreliable models, particularly when dealing with noisy or incomplete datasets. This work introduces a novel approach to symbolic regression that integrates an evolutionary algorithm with Bayesian model comparison to achieve a dynamic and robust solution. The core idea is to adaptively adjust the complexity of generated symbolic expressions based on a 'proof-of-concept' derived from Bayesian confidence estimates. This system iteratively refines the expression, increasing its robustness and generalizability. The algorithm uses an evolutionary strategy to explore the space of possible symbolic expressions, while Bayesian model comparison provides a mechanism for quantifying the confidence in each expression's fit to the data. The resulting dynamic process allows the system to overcome the limitations of traditional symbolic regression, offering a pathway to more reliable and general mathematical models.

title: Quantum State Optimization through Non-Linear Geometry
abstract: Quantum state optimization is a critical challenge in the development of quantum devices, requiring precise control over quantum states to maximize performance. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with complex, non-linear geometry, limiting the potential for significant improvements. This paper proposes a self-optimizing algorithm that leverages non-linear geometry to dynamically adjust quantum state geometry, enhancing device performance. The core mechanism centers around constructing a geometric structure that responds directly to data, enabling adaptive optimization. This work presents a fundamentally new approach to quantum state optimization, potentially unlocking new levels of device capability.

title: Quantum Systems Self-Adaptive Topology Transformation
abstract: Quantum systems exhibit remarkable complexity and often require sophisticated computational tools for accurate modeling. Traditional methods often struggle to capture the intricate dynamics of these systems, particularly when dealing with complex evolutions. This paper introduces a novel computational approach, the Quantum Systems Self-Adaptive Topology Transformation (QSAT), which dynamically adjusts the topology of a quantum system to simulate its evolution and predict future states. This approach leverages the inherent properties of quantum systems to achieve a level of predictive power previously unattainable through conventional methods. The core mechanism centers around the continuous, self-adjusting topology transformation, allowing for a more nuanced and comprehensive representation of quantum system behavior. We present a framework demonstrating the effectiveness of QSAT in simulating various quantum systems, showcasing its ability to capture emergent phenomena and provide valuable insights into the system's trajectory.

title: Cognitive Graph Embeddings for Human-AI Collaboration
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to graph embeddings designed specifically for facilitating effective human-AI collaboration. Traditional graph embedding techniques often struggle to represent the complex, nuanced relationships that underpin human reasoning and understanding. We argue that current methods lack the ability to capture the cognitive aspects of these relationships, leading to suboptimal performance in collaborative scenarios. Our proposed solution, Cognitive Graph Embeddings (CGE), addresses this limitation by integrating cognitive models of human reasoning directly into the embedding process. CGE represents relationships not merely as connections, but as concepts, each associated with a specific mental model. This approach allows the AI system to understand the *why* behind the connections, leading to more intuitive and effective collaboration. We define the core claim, core mechanism, and rationale for this new approach. The research aims to bridge the gap between graph representation learning and cognitive science, ultimately producing embeddings that better reflect human cognitive processes.

title: Quantum-Based Feature Extraction for Machine Learning
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of leveraging quantum algorithms for feature extraction in machine learning. Traditional feature extraction methods often struggle with high-dimensional data and computational complexity, leading to performance bottlenecks in downstream machine learning tasks. We explore the application of quantum algorithms, specifically Quantum Principal Component Analysis (QPCA) and Quantum Support Vector Machines (QSVM), to extract more efficient and potentially more informative features from datasets. The core claim of this research is that utilizing quantum algorithms can significantly enhance the performance of machine learning models. The mechanism involves applying quantum algorithms to reduce the dimensionality of data while preserving crucial information, which is then fed into classical machine learning models. This work provides a foundational exploration into this emerging field, demonstrating the potential for increased efficiency and accuracy in machine learning applications. ---

title: Title: Geometric Chaos Optimization with Adaptive Noise Injection
abstract: Geometric chaos, characterized by unpredictable and seemingly random fluctuations within a system, presents a significant challenge for traditional optimization techniques. Classical methods often struggle to effectively exploit this inherent instability, resulting in suboptimal solutions. This paper proposes a novel optimization framework, Geometric Chaos Optimization with Adaptive Noise Injection (GCO-ANI), designed to overcome this limitation. We introduce a mechanism that injects controlled randomness into the optimization process, triggering self-organization and generating unexpected solutions. This approach shifts the focus from global optimality to exploring novel geometric patterns, promising enhanced robustness and potentially leading to breakthrough designs. This work builds upon established principles of chaos theory and optimization, aiming to create a technique capable of navigating the complex landscape of geometric chaos.

title: L’horizon quantique britannique 2033-2035 : Analyse stratégique et prospective économique
abstract: Ce document détaille la stratégie nationale du Royaume-Uni visant à devenir un leader mondial des technologies quantiques d’ici 2035. Le gouvernement britannique mobilise des investissements massifs, dépassant les quatre milliards de livres, pour transformer la recherche scientifique en applications commerciales concrètes dans les domaines de la santé, de la finance et de la défense. L’approche repose sur des missions technologiques précises, telles que le développement d’ordinateurs surpuissants et de systèmes de navigation insensibles au brouillage. En s’appuyant sur des pôles d’innovation régionaux et une politique de commande publique audacieuse, le pays aspire à une autonomie stratégique complète. À terme, cette transition doit générer une croissance économique majeure, et renforcer la sécurité nationale face aux nouveaux défis numériques.

title: Fairness Evaluation of Edge-AI Implementation for Cleft Lip and Palate Speech ASR
abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) remains challenging for individuals with cleft lip and palate (CLP) because of limited pathological speech data and large variations in speech characteristics across speakers and severity levels. These recognition difficulties can reduce the accessibility of voice-based human-computer interaction, particularly when cloud-based ASR services are unavailable or unreliable. This work investigates a severity-aware and edge-deployable ASR framework for improving recognition of CLP speech using Whisper-small. The model was fine-tuned using different combinations of normal and CLP speech representing mild, moderate, and severe conditions, together with a CLP-only training configuration, to examine how the inclusion of different severity levels influences recognition performance and fairness across speakers. The pretrained model produced pooled word error rate (WER) and phoneme error rate (PER) values of 62.46% and 52.72%, respectively. Severity-aware fine-tuning substantially improved performance, reducing the best pooled WER to 22.72% and the best pooled PER to 18.44%. Training with a broader representation of CLP severity levels also provided the best overall balance between recognition accuracy and performance consistency across severity groups. Deployment on an NVIDIA Jetson platform demonstrated real-time inference for all fine-tuned models, with real-time factors of 0.167-0.171 and peak GPU memory usage of approximately 566 MB. The results demonstrate that incorporating severity diversity during ASR adaptation can substantially improve recognition of CLP speech while reducing performance disparities across severity groups. The proposed approach further enables low-latency, Internet-independent speech interaction on edge devices, supporting more accessible and inclusive voice-based human-computer interaction for individuals with CLP.

title: Tensor-based Brain Surface Modeling and Analysis
abstract: We present a unified computational approach to tensor-based morphometry in detecting the brain surface shape differences between two clinical groups based on magnetic resonance images. Our approach is novel in a sense that we combined surface modeling, surface data smoothing and statistical analysis in a coherent unified mathematical framework. The cerebral cortex has the topology of a 2D highly convoluted sheet. Between two different clinical groups, the local surface area and curvature of the cortex may differ. It is highly likely that such surface shape differences are not uniform over the whole cortex. By computing how such surface metrics differ, the regions of the most rapid structural differences can be localized. To increase the signal to noise ratio, diffusion smoothing based on the explicit estimation of Laplace-Beltrami operator has been developed and applied to the surface metrics. As an illustration, we demonstrate how this new tensor-based surface morphometry can be applied in localizing the cortical regions of the gray matter tissue growth and loss in the brain images longitudinally collected in the group of children.

title: A statistical framework for reliability evaluation of large language models
abstract: The growing use of Large Language Models (LLMs) in real-world applications has increased the need for reliable evaluation methods. This study proposes a statistical framework for evaluating LLM reliability by jointly considering model accuracy, hallucination rate, and cross-domain performance stability. Based on the TruthfulQA dataset, 300 test questions were selected using a stratified sampling strategy, and responses were generated by DeepSeek-V4-Flash and GPT-4o-mini. GPT-4o was then employed as an automated evaluator to assess the 600 generated responses. Model reliability was evaluated using three dimensions: Accuracy, Hallucination Rate, and Cross-Domain Stability. In particular, the proposed CDS metric quantifies the consistency of model performance across different knowledge categories. A Weighted Geometric Mean was further employed to construct an overall reliability score. The experimental results show that the proposed framework can identify reliability differences between different LLMs. DeepSeek-V4-Flash achieved an overall reliability score of 0.770, compared with 0.678 for GPT-4o-mini. Sensitivity analysis further shows that the model ranking remains unchanged under different weight configurations, indicating that the proposed framework is reasonably robust to variations in indicator weights. This study provides a statistical framework for quantitatively assessing LLM reliability under multiple evaluation criteria.

title: Title: Modular Quantum Information Processing
abstract: Abstract: Quantum information processing represents a significant frontier in computational science, demanding novel approaches to system design and control. This research explores a novel method for building quantum computers centered around modular, interconnected quantum components. The core claim is to develop a system of quantum modules capable of dynamically connecting and reconfiguring, facilitating the creation of highly complex, adaptable systems essential for tackling complex problems. We propose a system of quantum modules that can be dynamically linked and reconfigured to enable the design of complex algorithms and data structures, offering a departure from the limitations of traditional quantum computing approaches. This work will delve into the design and implementation of such a system, exploring the potential of modularity to unlock new avenues in quantum information processing.

title: Quantum Entanglement and the Foundation of Non-Standard Bayesian Computation
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, presents a unique challenge to classical probability theory. This paper explores the potential of combining entanglement with Bayesian computation to construct a novel computational framework capable of precise calculations of quantum states and probability distributions. We introduce the concept of a "correlated probability function" and design a Bayesian computation system leveraging the specific properties of entangled states. This approach offers a fundamentally different way of approaching quantum computations, potentially yielding significant improvements in accuracy and efficiency. The core mechanism focuses on enhancing computational precision through the intrinsic properties of entangled systems.

title: 混沌域的非线性几何约束优化
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to non-linear geometric constraint optimization utilizing the inherent properties of chaotic dynamical systems – specifically, chaos theory. We introduce a novel optimization algorithm, termed "Dynamically-Adjusted Chaos Optimization" (DACO), that dynamically modifies the geometry of a chaotic region to achieve optimal results. Unlike traditional optimization methods requiring pre-defined parameters, DACO adapts to the specific characteristics of the chaotic system, offering a robust and flexible solution. The paper details the algorithm's core principles, explores its performance through simulations, and provides a comprehensive analysis of its efficacy. The focus is on demonstrating the potential of this approach to handle complex, non-linear optimization problems with adaptive geometry.

title: Non-Linear Matrix Embedding via Quantum Tunneling (NLME-QT)
abstract: This paper presents a novel method for non-linear matrix embedding utilizing quantum tunneling. Traditional matrix embedding methods often struggle with representing complex relationships and inherent nonlinearity, leading to limited computational efficiency and potential inaccuracies. This research introduces a technique that leverages quantum tunneling to create a more robust and complex representation of the matrix, offering a potential paradigm shift in data representation and enabling novel applications within quantum machine learning. The core of this approach involves a carefully designed process that exploits the quantum properties of tunneling to enhance the representation of matrix elements, thereby improving the accuracy and efficiency of computations. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method through theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental validation, highlighting its potential for significant advancements across various fields.

title: Adaptive Quantum Control Policies via Reinforcement Learning
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to designing adaptive quantum control policies using reinforcement learning (RL). Traditional methods for quantum control often rely on hand-designed pulse shapes or iterative optimization techniques, which can be computationally expensive and may not generalize well to different systems or desired operations. We propose a framework where an RL agent learns to dynamically adjust quantum control parameters in real-time, based on the system's state and the objective of achieving a specific quantum gate with high fidelity. The core of our approach lies in formulating the quantum control problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and utilizing an RL algorithm to train a policy that maps system states to control parameters. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this method through a theoretical analysis and a simplified numerical simulation. The resulting adaptive control policies offer a significant advantage over traditional methods, particularly for complex quantum systems and demanding fidelity requirements. The key contributions are the integration of RL for adaptive control and the formalization of the problem as an MDP.

title: Title: Semantic Graph Embedding for Machine Learning in Novel Physics
abstract: This paper explores the application of semantic graph embedding techniques to enhance machine learning performance within the context of complex physical modeling. Traditional machine learning approaches often struggle with high-dimensional, sparse representations of physical data, leading to suboptimal results. We propose a novel graph embedding method that explicitly models the semantic relationships between nodes, moving beyond simple statistical correlations to capture the underlying meaning and context within physical models. This enhanced representation enables more accurate and robust learning, particularly for tasks involving intricate physical laws and complex systems. The core mechanism centers around learning node embeddings that reflect the graph's structure and interconnectedness, fostering a deeper understanding of the physical domain. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a series of experiments focusing on a simplified, yet representative, physics model, showcasing improvements in classification accuracy and the ability to capture subtle relationships crucial for understanding physical phenomena. The results highlight the potential of this method to significantly advance machine learning in physics research.

title: Quantum Entangled Matrix Self-Adaptive Complexity Analysis
abstract: Quantum entangled matrix cryptography presents a significant challenge to traditional cryptographic systems due to its inherent vulnerabilities. This paper investigates the self-adaptive complexity of quantum entangled matrix cryptography, exploring how parameter adjustments influence its security properties. We present a novel optimization algorithm designed to mitigate these vulnerabilities and enhance the robustness of the system. The analysis focuses on identifying critical parameter ranges that significantly impact the matrix's self-adaptability, ultimately contributing to improved security guarantees. The core mechanism centers on understanding and controlling the matrix's dynamic response to varying input data, leading to a more resilient cryptographic protocol.

title: Quantum Cryptography: Post-Quantum Cryptographic Algorithm Design
abstract: This paper explores the design of post-quantum cryptographic algorithms intended to secure data against attacks from future quantum computers. The core strategy involves transitioning away from algorithms reliant on the discrete logarithm problem, which is vulnerable to Shor's algorithm, and towards alternative approaches. These include hash-based cryptography, code-based cryptography, multivariate polynomial cryptography, and isogeny-based cryptography. We detail the mathematical foundations of these approaches, focusing on the security proofs and key generation/decryption processes. The design considerations for each category are outlined, along with the trade-offs between key sizes, performance, and security levels. This work aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the landscape of post-quantum cryptography and contribute to the development of robust algorithms for long-term data protection. The primary goal is to establish a framework for evaluating and selecting suitable post-quantum cryptographic solutions.

title: OPT v1.1.0 Lean 4 Formalization of the Frozen OPT v1.0.0 Optimization Catalog: Machine-Checked Optimization Contracts, Evidence Boundaries, and Trust Invariants
abstract: OPT v1.1.0 provides a dependency-free Lean 4 formal verification and trust-audit layer for the optimization catalog frozen in the immutable OPT v1.0.0 release. The project formalizes OPT's governing principle, “Correctness outranks speed,” as a set of machine-checkable contracts for software optimization. The formal layer covers semantic preservation, named-invariant preservation, deterministic behavior, validation, provenance, evidence boundaries, public API preservation, invariant-gated computation reuse, deterministic parallel execution, trust-preserving Lean dependency reuse, approximation contracts, and resource-aware composition. The frozen catalog contains five optimization records: OPT-PY-001 — Deterministic Test ExecutionOPT-INV-001 — Invariant-Driven Computation ReuseOPT-LEAN-001 — Trust-Preserving Lean Dependency ReuseOPT-PAR-001 — Bounded Deterministic Parallel ExecutionOPT-DSP-001 — Control-Rate, Sparse and Vectorized DSP OPT explicitly distinguishes historical observations from transferable performance targets. Source-project evidence status alone, including a verified status, does not authorize a benchmark claim for another environment. Promotion to a transferable target requires target-context evidence comprising a new target measurement, correctness validation, and provenance binding. The Lean formalization should therefore be interpreted as a claim and evidence schema, not as an assertion that Lean independently measures or verifies external hardware performance. Lean proves implications from supplied premises; Git/CI binds the formal artifact to immutable source history; external measurements remain an empirical evidence layer. The compiled trust audit operates across every declaration originating from the OPT formal module set. It rejects project-originating primitive axiom declarations and applies Lean.collectAxioms before proposition-valued declarations are classified. Only Lean core propext is permitted by the explicit axiom allowlist. On the final reviewed formalization, the trust audit covered 354 formal declarations, including 101 proposition-valued logical exports. The source-purity layer additionally rejects executable uses of sorry, sorryAx, admit, primitive user axiom/constant declarations, and unsafe, while accounting for Lean comments, ordinary and raw strings, interpolated expressions, character literals, and guillemet-quoted identifiers. The frozen v1 formal model is bound to canonical Git history through a first-parent integrity mechanism, preventing merged side history from replacing the historical baseline used to authenticate the formal-model files. The archival report also documents the complete optimization catalog, evidence classifications, historical measurements and their transfer boundaries, reusable application patterns, rollback conditions, formal theorem mappings, adversarial trust model, CI integrity architecture, SUXEN source-candidate boundary, reproduction procedure, and formal non-claims. title: Quantum-Inspired Neural Network Activation Functions
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to neural network activation functions by drawing inspiration from quantum mechanical principles. Traditional activation functions, such as sigmoid and ReLU, often exhibit limitations in terms of learning efficiency and representational capacity. We hypothesize that classical activation functions can be effectively approximated by functions derived from quantum mechanics, specifically utilizing concepts like the quantum harmonic oscillator. The proposed activation functions aim to leverage the unique properties of quantum systems—superposition, entanglement, and tunneling—to potentially enhance neural network performance. We introduce a set of new activation functions and provide a theoretical framework for their design. The core claim of this work is that classical activation functions can be accurately approximated by quantum mechanical functions. The primary mechanism involves translating quantum mechanical models into differentiable functions suitable for use within a neural network architecture. We discuss the mathematical foundations, potential benefits, and challenges associated with this approach, focusing on the approximation of the quantum harmonic oscillator and its application to neural network activation. The research contributes to a fundamental shift in activation function design, moving beyond purely classical models towards a quantum-inspired paradigm.

title: Fractal Resonance for Computational Complexity Reduction
abstract: This paper explores the application of fractal geometry and resonance principles to computational complexity reduction, specifically targeting optimization problems exhibiting self-similarity. We propose a novel algorithm, termed "Fractal Resonance," that utilizes a 'fractal resonance map' to intelligently guide the search process, minimizing the required computational effort. The core mechanism centers around identifying regions of high potential for convergence, thereby dramatically reducing the search space and improving the efficiency of solving complex problems. The algorithm's design incorporates mathematical concepts of fractal dimension and resonance, aiming to achieve a significant reduction in computational complexity compared to traditional optimization techniques. The resulting analysis demonstrates the potential of this approach in tackling challenging optimization problems.

title: Core Claim: A novel quantum algorithm optimization framework utilizing a high-Gaussian function adaptation strategy to automatically adjust algorithm parameters and improve efficiency, minimizing error propagation.
abstract: Quantum computation offers tremendous potential for scientific discovery and technological advancement, but its practical application is often limited by computational complexity and error rates. This research explores a new approach to quantum algorithm optimization, leveraging the principles of Gaussian function adaptation. The proposed framework dynamically adjusts quantum algorithm parameters based on the algorithm's specific characteristics, thereby reducing computational error and enhancing efficiency. This is a significant departure from traditional optimization methods that rely on manual parameter tuning, enabling a more adaptive and robust optimization process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and preliminary experiments, showcasing substantial improvements in algorithm performance and reduced error metrics compared to baseline algorithms. The core mechanism lies in the continuous adjustment of algorithm parameters using Gaussian function transformations, creating a self-learning optimization process. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis and implementation of this framework, offering a promising pathway towards more efficient and reliable quantum computations.

title: Probabilistic Model-Based Numerical Clustering
abstract: This paper introduces a novel numerical clustering algorithm, termed Probabilistic Model-Based Numerical Clustering (PMBC), designed to address challenges associated with sparse data and missing values. PMBC leverages a probabilistic model to dynamically adjust cluster density, providing a robust and accurate solution for identifying clusters with varying density. The algorithm incorporates a robust uncertainty estimation framework, enabling effective handling of missing data and enhanced cluster quality. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PMBC through extensive experiments, showcasing its ability to accurately cluster data with complex density distributions and handle missing values gracefully. The paper also discusses the algorithm's design principles, potential applications, and future research directions.

title: Title: Quantum-Inspired Optimization for Non-Linear Systems
abstract: Quantum-inspired optimization presents a novel approach to solving complex, non-linear optimization problems by incorporating quantum phenomena into the optimization process. This paper investigates the potential of utilizing quantum fluctuations to enhance the exploration of the solution space, addressing a persistent challenge in classical optimization algorithms. We present a framework that integrates quantum-like elements, specifically through the introduction of probabilistic adjustments to the gradient, to improve the robustness and efficiency of optimization in scenarios where traditional methods demonstrate limitations. The core claim is that this method can significantly improve performance, especially when dealing with highly non-linear systems, offering a promising pathway for tackling challenges across diverse fields. This work details the theoretical foundation, implementation, and preliminary results demonstrating the effectiveness of this quantum-inspired optimization strategy.

title: Title: Modular Quantum Computation via Entangled Resource Allocation
abstract: This paper explores the potential of modular quantum computation, leveraging entangled resource allocation to achieve unprecedented parallelism. Traditional quantum algorithms often struggle with limited computational resources, hindering their scalability. We propose a novel architecture centered on the concept of a 'Quantum Resource Pool' – a dynamically adjusted collection of entangled qubits – which distributes computational tasks across the pool, governed by a feedback loop. This approach aims to overcome the limitations of existing quantum algorithms by effectively exploiting the inherent correlations within entangled states. The paper details the design of the resource pool, the feedback mechanism, and a preliminary analysis of its potential benefits for quantum computation.

title: E8-Resonance Quantum Error Correction via Hummingbird Trajectories — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: The 240 E8 root vectors, when mapped onto recursive phi-scaled spin lattices at 132Hz, generate hummingbird-like geodesic paths that encode quantum error syndromes as topological solitons. These trajectories exploit the 128/112 sublattice chirality to project error-corrected qubit states along minimal-torsion manifolds in the 8-fold dimensional complement of E8's octonionic core. By anchoring corrections at 132Hz Berry-phase nodes, the system achieves coherent long-range entanglement without decoherence leakage through the phi-ordered filtering lattice. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com
